div.div: Programs talk to the terminal through the kernel’s tty API: termios (tcgetattr/tcsetattr) and ioctl. Those calls only succeed on a real tty file descriptor. So the terminal emulator can’t just hand over a pipe and implement the behavior itself, because isatty() would be false and tcsetattr would fail.

text.tspan: Programs talk to the terminal through the kernel’s tty API: termios (tcgetattr/tcsetattr)
and ioctl. Those calls only succeed on a real tty file descriptor. So the terminal
emulator can’t just hand over a pipe and implement the behavior itself, because
isatty() would be false and tcsetattr would fail.

div.div:
When text is printed, the terminal writes characters into this grid at the current cursor position and advances the cursor. If text hits the edge of the screen, the grid either wraps or scrolls up.
like: - cursor position, current “pen” style, scroll region, tab stops, the scrollback buffer, and the alternate screen (what vim and less switch to, so your shell history comes back when you quit).

div.div:
It takes the Unicode code point (e.g., U+0041 for 'A').
It queries the operating system's font shaping engine (like FreeType on Linux, CoreText on macOS, or DirectWrite on Windows) and requests the vector outline for that character from your active terminal font.

It queries the operating system's font shaping engine (like FreeType
on Linux, CoreText on macOS, or DirectWrite on Windows) and

div.div: The Optimization (Glyph Atlases): Rendering vector outlines for every single character on every frame would destroy CPU performance. Instead, terminals use a glyph cache. Frequently used characters are rendered once into a texture atlas (a GPU memory sheet), and the terminal treats them as pre-rendered bitmap textures

text.tspan: The Optimization (Glyph Atlases): Rendering vector outlines for every
single character on every frame would destroy CPU performance.
Instead, terminals use a glyph cache. Frequently used characters are
rendered once into a texture atlas (a GPU memory sheet), and the
terminal treats them as pre-rendered bitmap textures

div.p: The incoming bytes are decoded as UTF-8 into code points. This is where mismatched encodings produce gibberish, as in the first question.

text.tspan: Decoding
The incoming bytes are decoded as UTF-8 into code
points. This is where mismatched encodings produce
gibberish, as in the first question.

div.p: The bytes mix printable text and control codes, which are instructions rather than text:

ul.li: C0 controls: \n (move down), \r (cursor to column 0), \b (back one), \t (tab), \a (bell)

Escape sequences starting with ESC (0x1B):
CSI ESC [ ... such as ESC[31m (red text), ESC[2;5H (move cursor to row 2, col 5), ESC[2J (clear screen)
OSC ESC ] ... such as setting the window title or making hyperlinks
DCS and others for things like Sixel images

text.tspan: Parsing the stream
The bytes mix printable text and control codes, which are instructions rather than text:
C0 controls: \n (move down), \r (cursor to column 0), \b (back one), \t (tab), \a (bell)
Escape sequences starting with ESC (0x1B):
CSI ESC [ ... such as ESC[31m (red text), ESC[2;5H (move cursor to row 2, col 5), ESC[2J (clear screen)
OSC ESC ] ... such as setting the window title or making hyperlinks
DCS and others for things like Sixel images

div.div:
modern GPU terminals (Alacritty, Kitty, WezTerm, Ghostty) cache rasterized glyphs in a texture atlas and draw one textured quad per cell with OpenGL, Metal, or Vulkan.
Older ones like xterm draw with CPU-side calls

div.div:
. A PTY isn’t needed to talk to a shell, it’s needed to make the shell and the programs it runs behave interactively
echo "ls -l" | bash // no pty required
So the PTY is a compatibility layer. It exists so a program written for a 1970s serial terminal still works unchanged when the “terminal” is a window on your screen.

text.tspan: . A PTY isn’t needed to talk to a shell, it’s needed to make the shell and the
programs it runs behave interactively
echo "ls -l" | bash // no pty required
So the PTY is a compatibility layer. It exists so a program written for a 1970s
serial terminal still works unchanged when the “terminal” is a window on your
screen.

Terminal emulator (Alacritty, Kitty, Windows Terminal, GNOME Terminal...)
├─ 1. Decode bytes (UTF-8) into code points
